title.rendered: His Mercy Endures Forever: The Refrain That Never Ends | The Thankful Heart, Day 12

excerpt.rendered: Psalm 136:1 calls us to give thanks to the Lord, for His mercy endures forever. Day 12 of The Thankful Heart joins the refrain that never ends.

content.rendered:
Twenty-six verses, and every single one ends the same way: for His mercy endures forever. Psalm 136 is not repetitive by accident. It is a song designed so that no one could ever forget the chorus.

The Gospel For Today | Thursday, November 26, 2026 | The Thankful Heart, Day 12

Today’s Scripture

“Oh, give thanks to the Lord, for He is good! For His mercy endures forever.”
Psalm 136:1 (NKJV)

“Who remembered us in our lowly state, for His mercy endures forever; and rescued us from our enemies, for His mercy endures forever; who gives food to all flesh, for His mercy endures forever. Oh, give thanks to the God of heaven! For His mercy endures forever.”
Psalm 136:23-26 (NKJV)

The Original Word: Mercy

חָ֫סֶד (chesed, Hebrew, Strong’s H2617)

The word the NKJV renders “mercy” is chesed (pronounced KHEH-sed), a masculine noun used about 247 times in the Old Testament. Its range of meaning includes lovingkindness, mercy, steadfast love, loyalty, faithfulness and goodness. In Psalm 136:1, as in every verse of this psalm, it describes the Lord’s own kindness toward His people. The KJV also says “mercy”, the NASB says “lovingkindness” and the ESV says “steadfast love”. Each version is reaching for one side of a word that holds several together.

In everyday English, “mercy” usually means kindness shown to someone who does not deserve it, and that is part of chesed. But the Hebrew lexicons describe God’s chesed at work in rescue from enemies, in preserving life, in redemption from sin and in keeping covenant. It is kindness with loyalty inside it, love that has bound itself by promise. That is why the psalm can say it endures forever. In Jesus, God kept His covenant promise in full, and the cross shows a chesed that has already done everything needed to rescue us.

Today’s Message

Today many of our friends in the United States are gathering around tables for Thanksgiving Day. Wherever you are in the world, from Lagos to London to Manila, it is a fitting day to sing the oldest thanksgiving song of all. Psalm 136 was likely sung in the temple as a call and response. A leader would sing the first line of each verse, and the people would answer with one voice: “For His mercy endures forever.”

Look at how the psalm moves. It starts with who God is: good, the God of gods, the Lord of lords. Then it moves to creation: the heavens, the earth, the sun, the moon and the stars. Then to history: the rescue from Egypt, the parting of the sea, the journey through the wilderness, the gift of the land. And finally it comes close and personal: “Who remembered us in our lowly state.” After every line, great or small, the same answer: His mercy endures forever.

This chesed is the steadfast love of a God who has bound Himself to His people by promise. And the psalm says it endures forever. It does not run out in a bad year. It does not expire when we fail. It outlasts every enemy and every season.

For us, that steadfast love has a name and a face. It is Jesus. In Him God remembered us in our lowly state. In Him we were rescued from every enemy, including sin and death. Titus 3:5 says He saved us not by works of righteousness which we have done, but according to His mercy. The chorus of Psalm 136 found its final verse at the cross and the empty tomb.

So today, try writing your own Psalm 136. List what God has done in your life this year, line by line. After each one, write or say the chorus: for His mercy endures forever. The promotion and the disappointment. The provision and the waiting. The friends who came and the ones who went. You will find that every line of your story ends the same way.

How the Thankful Heart Sings the Chorus

It starts with who God is. Give thanks to the Lord, for He is good.

It sees His mercy in every line. Creation, history and our own story all end with the same refrain.

It finds the chorus in Christ. His steadfast love remembered us and rescued us through Jesus.

Declaration

Lord, I give thanks to You, for You are good, and Your mercy endures forever (Psalm 136:1). I thank You that You remembered me in my lowly state and rescued me from my enemies through Jesus (Psalm 136:23-24). I thank You that You saved me, not by works of righteousness I have done, but according to Your mercy (Titus 3:5). In every line of my story, Your steadfast love is there, and it will never run out. In Jesus’ name. Amen.
